paper_title: SIMIT: Self-Improving Vision-Language Models via Imagination at Test-Time

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce SIMIT, a test-time self-improvement framework in which a vision-language model creates its own query-specific training data before answering an unlabeled test query. Our goal is to improve performance on a given target test set without annotations or external models. To pursue this goal, some test-time methods improve answers through longer reasoning or repeated sampling but leave the model unchanged. Others update the model using rewards based on majority agreement among multiple candidate answers or the model's own judgments of correctness, but such rewards can reinforce existing mistakes. SIMIT instead imagines similar problems whose solutions it controls: a model need not correctly solve the target query to construct useful practice examples. It synthesizes diverse (question, answer, image) triplets by specifying each answer before realizing its image. To support diverse multimodal tasks, SIMIT combines native image generation with an extensible skill library for structured visuals, including documents, charts, and diagrams. Within this pipeline, multi-stage verification checks that images support their assigned answers, while difficulty filtering retains informative examples. Adaptive budgeting further targets this practice by allocating more samples to queries the model is less confident in answering. The resulting data can improve the model in-context (SIMIT-ICL) or in-weight (SIMIT-FT). Across 17 diverse benchmarks, SIMIT outperforms existing self-improvement methods. Its best configuration achieves a +7.20% mean relative gain over BAGEL-7B, while training-free SIMIT-ICL achieves +6.98%.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: The success of vision-language models (VLMs) depends on expensive human-labeled data for generalpurpose pretraining and task-focused post-training (Dai et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024). One issue with this training strategy is that models cannot anticipate every task, domain, or failure mode encountered in real-world use after deployment. In this paper, we study the problem of test-time self-improvement, where VLM can improve its performance on an unlabeled dataset, without access to an external teacher or additional human-annotated data. Such capability would enable VLM to specialize its abilities on demand, using the input data itself to determine what it needs to learn. Test-time scaling offers partial solution to this problem. Longer thinking, repeated sampling, and majority voting can improve frozen models predictions (Wei et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023) without providing persistent parameter updates for subsequent queries. An alternative approach is test-time training, which updates model weights using pseudo-labels or rewards derived from confidence, consensus, or self-rewarding (Huang et al., 2023; Zuo et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2024). This enables cross-query transfer, but supervision comes from the response behavior being corrected, which can reinforce systematic errors (Wei et al., 2026b; He et al., 2026a). Furthermore, open-ended multimodal tasks present an additional problem: semantically equivalent answers may differ in wording, complicating voting-based solutions, while verification requires checking fine-grained visual evidence. Retrieval-based methods, such as RICES (Alayrac et al., 2022) and TTT-NN (Hardt & Sun, 2024), offer another source of supervision by adapting from humanannotated examples. However, they require access to labeled retrieval set that is not available in our label-free problem setting. Taken together, these limitations motivate the need for source of supervision that requires neither correctly answering the target test query nor access to labeled data.

sections.content: Figure 1: (Left) SIMIT. Given an unlabeled test query 1 , the VLM imagines similar samples 2 , uses them to improve itself via in-context learning or by fine-tuning 3 , and answers the original test query with the self-improved model 4 . No labels or external models are used. (Right) Mean relative gain versus runtime across 17 benchmarks. In this paper, we tackle the problem of test-time self-improvement by synthesizing input-relevant supervision samples using the underlying model itself  (Fig. 1)  . Our approach aims to synthesize useful, accurate, and diverse questionanswerimage triplets, conditioned on given test query. SIMIT achieves these goals using unified multimodal models (UMMs), which have image understanding and generation capabilities that enable the same model to synthesize and learn from its own multimodal samples without target labels or external models. But existing UMMs can only generate natural images and struggle with structured visuals, e.g., documents, charts, and diagrams (Wei et al., 2026a). Addressing this weakness, SIMIT can synthesize variety of image types with an extensible library of structured rendering skills. In order to minimize unnecessary computation, the synthesis budget is allocated adaptively, based on the confidence of the UMM in its zero-shot response. The generated samples are checked for internal consistency and filtered based on their expected difficulty. The synthesized samples can be used in two modes for self-improvement: SIMIT-FT uses them for finetuning, while SIMIT-ICL uses them as in-context demonstrations without model parameter access. With access to single test query, we use SIMIT-ICL or SIMIT-FT (Single-Query). But with access to multiple test queries, SIMIT-FT (Test-Set) allows the performance gained for one query to benefit others. SIMIT-FTICL combines both using the finetuned model with few-shot prompting. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: Imagination-based self-supervision. The same model creates its own query-conditioned training samples by imagining similar problems, without predicting labels for the original test inputs. General multimodal realization. We combine the models native image generation with structured rendering skills, multi-stage verification, difficulty filtering, and confidence-adaptive budget allocation to build query-conditioned synthetic data spanning natural and structured visual tasks. Flexible adaptation and broad evaluation. We can use the self-generated samples for in-context learning and single-query or test-set finetuning. Across 17 benchmarks with BAGEL-7B (Deng et al., 2025), mean relative gains over zero-shot are 6.98% for SIMIT-ICL, 1.69% for single-query SIMIT-FT, 6.39% for test-set SIMIT-FT, and 7.20% for SIMIT-FTICL, outperforming prior work. Our synthetic data can even outperform human-annotated data on some benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) improves answers by spending more computation when solving query. Sequential methods think step-by-step (chain-of-thought, Wei et al., 2022) or repeatedly critique and revise an answer (Self-Refine, Madaan et al., 2023). Parallel methods generate multiple candidate solutions, then choose the majority-voted answer (Self-Consistency, Wang et al., 2023) or score the candidates and select the best one (best-of-K) (Cobbe et al., 2021; Snell et al., 2025). However,

sections.content: approaches that score using external reward models fall outside our self-contained problem setting. But self-contained aggregation can reinforce the models biases and lack meaningful consensus on open-ended tasks such as captioning. Also, conventional TTS leaves model parameters unchanged. Computation spent on one query does not benefit subsequent queries. SIMIT instead converts test-time compute into query-conditioned practice data, enabling in-context or in-weight adaptation. Label-Free Reinforcement Learning (LFRL) updates the model parameters using intrinsic rewards. TTRL rewards majority agreement (Zuo et al., 2025), TTRV uses response frequencies and entropy regularization (Singh et al., 2026), and EMPO uses semantic clustering (Zhang et al., 2026), which may require an external model. SRLM instead uses self-judging rewards (Yuan et al., 2024), limited by evaluation capability and vulnerable to reward hacking (Gao et al., 2023). Cross-query transfer and online reward updates can improve pseudo-labels beyond the initial majority vote (Zuo et al., 2025), but isolated single query adaptation lacks this transfer. MM-UPT additionally synthesizes questions around existing images while retaining majority-derived supervision (Wei et al., 2026b). SIMIT instead specifies answers before constructing and verifying new visual inputs. Test-Time Training (TTT) adapts parameters using either retrieved neighbors (Hardt & Sun, 2024), supervision from augmented demonstrations or test inputs (Akyürek et al., 2025; Kaya et al., 2026), or likelihood objectives on unlabeled inputs (Hu et al., 2025). Closest to SIMIT, TT-SI (Acikgoz et al., 2026) finetunes on self-generated tool-use examples, validating calls and selecting function labels by majority agreement. SIMIT constructs complete multimodal examples without labeled retrieval corpus or supplied demonstrations. Extended related work can be found in Appendix B.

sections.title: 3 METHODS
sections.content: 3.1 PROBLEM FORMULATION: TEST-TIME SELF-IMPROVEMENT Given vision-language model πθ and an unlabeled target test set = {(Ii, qi)}N i=1, we aim to improve performance on the target distribution without its ground-truth answers. We study self-contained setting: πθ is the only learned model available at test time, with no auxiliary teacher, verifier, retriever, or generator. Deterministic tools and renderers may execute model-produced specifications, but all semantic decisions and supervision originate from πθ. This problem setting measures whether the model can reorganize its existing latent capabilities for self-improvement. The setting is label-free and target-conditioned. Unlike conventional SFT, RLVR, and RLHF, supervision comes from the target model πθ rather than ground-truth targets, externally specified verifiable rewards, or human preferences. Moreover, unlike untargeted zero-data self-improvement (He et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026), observed target queries determine what the model should practice in our problem setting, focusing self-improvement on specific target. 3.2 SELF-SUPERVISION BY IMAGINING SIMILAR PROBLEMS SIMIT self-improves on an unlabeled test query by constructing similar multimodal samples and using them for adaptation. Its central idea is question-answer-guided image generation: the model first proposes new questions and their intended answers, then generates images to support those answers. This avoids directly reusing incorrect predictions on the test query as supervision. The remaining challenge is to make the resulting samples valid and useful for the models own adaptation. Our synthesis pipeline  (Fig. 2)  is designed to produce accurate, diverse, and informative examples (see App. for formal argument). The process begins with Adaptive Budget Allocation, which selects synthesis budget from the models initial confidence on the test query. Triplet Synthesis then generates diverse triplets {(qk, ak, dk)}K k=1, question, intended answer, and image description, conditioned on the test query (Ii, qi). Visualization Routing selects the models own native image generation or suitable structured rendering skill for each description dk. Image Realization generates the corresponding image Ik. Verification checks whether each image supports its question-answer pair, triggering repair or regeneration when needed. Finally, Difficulty Filtering uses the models confidence in the intended answers ak to discard samples that are too easy or difficult. Adaptive Budget Allocation. Different test queries require different amounts of practice. We select query-specific synthesis budget based on the models confidence in its zero-shot prediction.

Confidence is the mean token probability of the models zero-shot answer, and decreases monotonically with confidence. Appendix derives our allocation rule and optimal functional form. Triplet Synthesis. Conditioned on the test image and question (Ii, qi), the model proposes synthetic triplets (qk, ak, dk): question, its intended answer, and textual description of an image that would support that answer. Diversity-encouraging prompting promotes variation while preserving the target task and its answer format. Each answer is committed before its image is generated, turning label acquisition into conditional construction. Generating both questions and images expands practice beyond fixed test image. We use UMM to generate images without an external model. Visualization Routing. The next step is to turn each textual description dk into an image Ik. But we cannot simply use the models native image generation capabilities, as existing UMMs are incapable of generating structured images (Wei et al., 2026a). They struggle with the precise text, quantities, and spatial relations required by structured visuals  (Fig. 5)  . Thus, we prompt the same model to identify each descriptions visualization category. Based on this classification, we route natural-image requests to native generation and structured-image requests to category-specific rendering skills. Image Realization. For structured visuals, directly generating Python/LATEX/HTML code demands programming, layout, and geometric reasoning capabilities that current UMMs may not reliably possess. Whereas prior work develops structured generation capabilities through finetuning or reinforcement learning (Chen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025), our skill library uses modular instructions, easy-to-use interfaces, and reusable rendering resources without training (Xu & Yan, 2026). Each skill guides the model to produce compact specification, such as geometric primitives or graph nodes and edges. deterministic backend parses it and computes supported quantities, geometry, and layout, enabling syntax checks and explicit error feedback. For example, to draw regular pentagon inscribed in circle, the model only specifies the center, radius, and number of sides, and the renderer computes vertices and requested angle labels consistently. Skills can also compose, e.g., the HTML skill can embed natively generated images. The skill library covers common benchmark tasks. Fig. 3 shows representative outputs. It is easily extensible with additional specifications and backends. Appendix provides implementation details, such as prompts, interfaces, rendering backends, etc. Verification. App. derives our band-pass rule from an expected utility formulation. 3.3 TEST-TIME UPDATE: USE CASES OF THE SELF-GENERATED SYNTHETIC DATA The self-generated data can be used for in-context learning (SIMIT-ICL), fine-tuning (SIMIT-FT), or both. We study the following use cases to reflect practical scenarios with different constraints. SIMIT-ICL uses synthesized samples directly as few-shot demonstrations (Brown et al., 2020). Self-generated demonstrations have been explored for text-only LLMs through SG-ICL, SELF-ICL, and analogical prompting (Kim et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023; Yasunaga et al., 2024). SIMIT additionally uses synthesized visual inputs for the generated questionanswer pairs and verifies their consistency. SIMIT-ICL is prompting technique requiring only inference access. It is suitable for API-accessible models and settings where fine-tuning is infeasible. SIMIT-FT (Single-Query, SQ) treats each test query as separate = 1 adaptation problem. We finetune the base model on query-specific synthetic examples, answer the query, and reset before the next query. This offers complementary axis of test-time scaling: spending computation on query-specific learning instead of conventional parallel or sequential scaling. It suits requests that prioritize accuracy over latency and applications that restrict information retention: synthetic data can be discarded after answering, and parameter updates do not persist across queries. SIMIT-FT (Test-Set, TS) combines synthetic examples from all test queries to finetune the model before evaluating it on the target test set. This allows the supervision generated for one query to benefit others. It has many applications, such as automatic labeling and LLM personalization. SIMIT-FTICL first finetunes on the self-generated data and then supplies them as in-context demos to the finetuned model. It combines weight adaptation with query-specific contextual guidance.

See Appendix for more qualitative samples. Retrieval-based methods are bottlenecked by dataset coverage. Self-generated demos, targeted to the query, recover from it without requiring annotated retrieval sets. Test-Time Scaling. Self-Consistency provides modest gains, while Self-Refine often reduces performance. BAGELs thinking mode degrades scores, even with 10,000-token budget, consistent with recent evidence that excess test-time generation can hurt perception-focused tasks through overthinking and hallucination (Sammani et al., 2026). Inspection reveals thinking mode yields overly verbose captions and instruction-following failures regarding the expected answer format. Single-Query Adaptation. Our theoretical analysis shows that consensus-based LFRL (TTRL, EMPO, TTRV) cannot reliably improve on the initial majority-vote prediction under isolated singlequery adaptation (Appendix F). Thus, we evaluate LFRL only in the test-set setting. Their performance gains in the test-set adaptation setting are largely due to cross-sample capability transfer. SIMIT-FT (SQ) and SIMIT-ICL improve performance even when each query is adapted in isolation. Consensus Reinforces Systematic Errors. The base model often outputs unanswerable even for answerable queries, incorrectly claiming insufficient visual information (e.g., Fig. 4). TTRL reinforces such biases: unanswerable is the majority vote in 99.2% of training steps for VizWiz. Only few steps yield nonzero group-relative advantages, and 79.3% of those still reinforce unanswerable. Thus, consensus rewards can perpetuate the models biases rather than provide corrective supervision. Generalization. Separately, we also test SIMITs generalization across models (Appendix K) and benchmarks (Appendix J). SIMIT-ICL improves over the zero-shot baseline by +2.21% on SenseNova-U1 (Diao et al., 2026) and +3.97% on Lance (Fu et al., 2026), showing that the gains extend beyond BAGEL. In the cross-benchmark experiments, transfer yields mean relative gains of 4.3% within domains and 0.5% across domains, although target-specific adaptation remains stronger. This demonstrates the importance of targeted self-improvement and query-conditioned synthesis. In-context and in-weight adaptation offer complementary gains: ICL leads on 8 benchmarks and test-set FT on 9. Their combination performs best overall. ICL does not require weight updates or access to the whole test set. Test-set FT outperforms isolated FT, due to cross-sample transfer. 4.2 COMPARISON OF SELF-GENERATED SYNTHETIC DATA VS. sections.title: 4.4 WHY DOES SIMIT OUTPERFORM LFRL?
sections.content: We distinguish supervision quality from its utility. Models may fail to benefit from correct supervision, while incorrect supervision may be less harmful in queries they already answer confidently and correctly. We therefore first measure how often adaptation corrects initial errors or disrupts correct predictions, and then assess the correctness of supervision and whether its errors concentrate where the model already fails. Stratified Gain Analysis. We split test queries by whether Self-Consistency (K = 32) answers correctly, then measure the correction rate among initially wrong queries and the disruption rate among initially correct ones, reporting their difference as = (wrong correct) (correct wrong). As shown in Fig. 6, SIMIT corrects 14.4% of initially wrong queries while disrupting only 2.0% of initially correct ones (=+12.4pp). The strongest LFRL baseline, TTRV, corrects only 9.3% at the same disruption rate, and others correct even fewer ( +5.3pp). Their gains over the zero-shot baseline thus combine smaller net correction with the majority-vote gain, which sharpening preserves by stabilizing low-margin correct predictions. SIMITs advantage lies in correcting more errors, not in preserving more correct predictions. This gap follows from how consensus-based methods operate: they reward agreement and also predict by majority vote, so training mainly sharpens predictions the majority already answers correctly. Such prediction-derived supervision can reinforce existing errors (Wang et al., 2026). In contrast, SIMITs imagination-based, independently realized supervision offers route to correct them. Both the overall rate of such errors and whether they concentrate on queries the base model already fails matter. To measure this, for each method, we sample one positively-encouraged pseudo-label per query following its own reward rule. Then, an external blind evaluator (Claude Sonnet 5) judges their correctness. Writing L=1 for incorrect supervision and =1 for base-model error on the same query, δ = (L=1 =1) (L=1 =0) measures whether supervision errors concentrate where the model already fails. On queries the base model answers incorrectly, SIMITs supervision is correct far more often than it is incorrect, while every LFRL baseline shows the reverse  (Fig. 7)  . SIMITs overall supervision-error rate is also roughly third of every baselines (12% vs. 3338%), and its δ is small and negative (6.5pp) whereas δ is large and positive for all LFRL baselines (+22 to +79pp; Appendix L). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: SIMIT creates query-specific multimodal self-supervision by specifying answers before constructing the corresponding images, allowing VLM to learn without first solving the target test query. Combining finetuning with ICL achieves +7.20% mean gain over BAGEL-7B baseline without any annotations or extra models. This turns test-time compute into targeted practice, offering route to more accurate automatic annotation and personalized agents learning from the tasks they encounter.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: To ensure the replicability of our findings, we release our code, allowing the research community to reproduce our results and build upon our contributions. Our experimental setup is based on publicly accessible models, ensuring that all resources are readily obtainable by other researchers. We provide comprehensive details regarding the prompts and hyperparameters utilized across our experiments in Appendix G. Also, Appendix contains thorough descriptions of the benchmarks employed in our study. All evaluation benchmarks utilized in this work are established and widely used standards within the field. Our commitment to transparency extends beyond code release, as we meticulously detail every aspect of our experimental methodology to enable faithful reproduction of our work.

sections.title: AUTHOR STATEMENT ON THE USE OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
sections.content: During the preparation of this paper, large language models were used solely for language polishing and coding assistance. They were not used for research ideation, experiment design, analysis, or writing of scientific content. All research contributions are the sole responsibility of the authors. As part of our method, we also use vision-language models to generate synthetic training datasets.

sections.title: A DATASET STATISTICS
sections.content: We evaluate on 17 benchmarks across five domains using LMMs-Eval-Lite (Zhang et al., 2025a), compact evaluation suite derived from LMMs-Eval. It uses coreset selection to retain representative examples, reducing evaluation cost while preserving broad task coverage. The original study reports strong correlations between scores on the selected subsets and the corresponding full benchmarks, supporting their use for efficient evaluation and ablation studies. Tab. 4 summarizes our datasets and sample counts. Table 4: LMMs-Eval Lite with additional datasets. Task Domain Dataset Retrieval/Training Val. Eval. Image Understanding & Captioning Visual Question Answering Flickr30k (Young et al., 2014) NoCaps (Agrawal et al., 2019) TextCaps (Sidorov et al., 2020) RefCOCO (Kazemzadeh et al., 2014) COCO (Lin et al., 2014) GQA (Hudson & Manning, 2019) OK-VQA (Marino et al., 2019) VizWiz-VQA (Gurari et al., 2018) VQA-v2(-Small) (Goyal et al., 2017) TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019) Math & Science AI2D (Kembhavi et al., 2016) Document & Infographic Understanding Multi-discipline Total ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022) DocVQA (Mathew et al., 2021) InfoVQA (Mathew et al., 2022) MM-Bench (CN) (Liu et al., 2024) MM-Bench (EN) (Liu et al., 2024) SEED-Bench (Li et al., 2023) 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 2000 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 50 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 500 34000 850 8500 For each benchmark, we use 50 validation examples and 500 evaluation examples, totaling 850 and 8,500 examples, respectively. Validation sets support hyperparameter selection for SIMIT and all baseline methods. For SIMIT, validation data determine the adaptive-budget parameters (ε, A0, A1, B, Kmax) and difficulty-filtering thresholds (Tlow, Thigh), with Bayesian optimization used for hyperparameter search. We fix the selected hyperparameter configurations before reporting results on the evaluation sets. Ground-truth answers from the evaluation set are used only for scoring. All methods operate on unlabeled queries. Each benchmark also provides pool of 2,000 annotated retrieval/training examples, totaling 34,000 examples. These pools support the real-versus-synthetic comparisons in Sec. 4.2: they supply retrieved in-context demonstrations, retrieved neighbors for single-query finetuning, and training examples for test-set finetuning. SIMIT uses its own synthetic examples as adaptation supervision. We use CIDEr for all five Image Understanding & Captioning benchmarks. CIDEr measures agreement with reference human-annotated descriptions through TFIDF-weighted n-gram similarity (Vedantam et al., 2015). The five VQA benchmarks and AI2D use exact-match accuracy. ChartQA uses relaxed accuracy, which tolerates small numerical deviations, while DocVQA and InfoVQA use average normalized Levenshtein similarity (ANLS), which allows partial credit for small characterlevel differences. MMBench (CN/EN) and SEED-Bench use multiple-choice accuracy. Higher scores indicate better performance for every metric. Captioning scores are reported in native CIDEr units, and all other scores are expressed on 0-100 scale. Domain scores are arithmetic means across constituent benchmarks, with relative improvements computed from the domain averages. To aggregate across heterogeneous metrics, overall gains are computed as the mean of benchmark-level relative improvements over the zero-shot baseline across all 17 benchmarks, giving each benchmark equal weight.

Bold text describes method family, followed by representative methods where applicable. (A) Labels before deployment: whether labeled examples of the target task are available beyond pretraining (A1) or not (A2). (B) Test-time access to the target: whether the method sees each test query in isolation (B1), the unlabeled test set as batch or stream (B2), or no test data or no estimation of the test distribution, so all adaptation happens before deployment (B3). sections.title: B EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) methods improve predictions by allocating additional inference compute (Zhang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025b). This compute can be deployed along two main axes. Sequential methods extend or revise an evolving solution trajectory through scratchpad or chainof-thought reasoning, budget forcing, or iterative self-feedback (Nye et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Madaan et al., 2023). Parallel methods sample multiple candidate responses and either aggregate them through self-consistency or majority voting, or select one using verifier or reward model, as in best-of-K (Wang et al., 2023; Cobbe et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2025; Jeddi et al., 2026). However, not all TTS methods are compatible with our problem setting: approaches requiring externally trained verifiers or reward models introduce supervision excluded by test-time self-improvement, which assumes neither labels nor external models. Self-contained TTS methods can elicit latent competence, particularly on verifiable tasks. Nevertheless, their gains depend on the base models generative support and the reliability of the aggregation or selection signal. For instance, majority voting improves over single prediction when each candidate response is correct with probability > 0.5. But when < 0.5, it amplifies the prevailing error (Wei et al., 2026b). This limitation is even more pronounced for open-ended tasks such as image captioning, where sampled responses are typically all distinct; consequently, no majority exists, and voting

More fundamentally, conventional TTS leaves the model unchanged: computation spent on one query does not directly correct underlying misconceptions or benefit subsequent queries. SIMIT instead converts test-time compute into verified, query-conditioned practice data, enabling adaptation in context or in weight space. Label-Free Reinforcement Learning (LFRL) closes the loop left open by inference-only TTS: instead of discarding sampled responses after aggregation, it converts model-intrinsic signals into pseudo-rewards and updates the model on unlabeled test data. Earlier self-training methods fit high-confidence, self-consistent solutions using SFT (Huang et al., 2023), whereas TTRL uses the majority-voted answer as pseudo-label and rewards agreement with it through GRPO (Zuo et al., 2025). TTRV extends this paradigm to VLMs using frequency-proportional rewards and entropy regularization (Singh et al., 2026). The failures of majority voting are even more consequential under LFRL: when open-ended responses such as captions are all distinct, an arbitrary pseudo-label is selected and then reinforced through training. Semantic clustering-based approaches, such as EMPO, relax exact matching (Zhang et al., 2026), but free-form clustering may require an auxiliary model, violating our setting. Most closely related to SIMIT, MM-UPT additionally synthesizes questions around existing images; however, it neither generates new visual inputs nor constructs their answers, and still derives supervision through majority voting (Wei et al., 2026b). Because rewards are recomputed online, these methods can surpass the initial models majority-vote accuracy: parameter sharing enables cross-query transfer, and the updated policy can produce better pseudolabels in later iterations (Zuo et al., 2025). Nevertheless, their supervision remains highly coupled to the models own beliefs. Recent analysis shows that certaintyand consistency-based intrinsic rewards primarily sharpen the models initial output distribution (He et al., 2026a). Despite their different reward formulations, all these methods remain fundamentally consensus-based and therefore inherit the limitations of the models sampled answer distribution. Such reinforcement is useful only when confidence aligns with correctness, but can also amplify systematic biases. For example, generic deflection such as unanswerable may be reinforced whenever it dominates the sampled responses, even for answerable queries. MM-UPT similarly demonstrates that intrinsic rewards can amplify errors on deliberately difficult data when the model lacks relevant prior knowledge (Wei et al., 2026b). This dependence on the models existing beliefs is particularly restrictive under query-isolated single-query adaptation: cross-query transfer is unavailable, and reinforcing consensus provides no independent signal for correcting an initially wrong majority. An orthogonal approach is to use self-judging rewards, where the model evaluates the correctness of its own responses, as in SRLM (Yuan et al., 2024). However, such rewards remain bounded by the models own evaluation capabilities and are vulnerable to reward hacking (Gao et al., 2023). SIMIT instead specifies each answer before visual realization and subsequently verifies the resulting triplet, decoupling supervision from the solvers current answer distribution. Test-Time Training (TTT) updates model parameters during inference to specialize on an observed input or target distribution (Sun et al., 2020), motivated by the earlier works on local and transductive learning (Bottou & Vapnik, 1992; Joachims, 1999). The central challenge is obtaining reliable supervision aligned with the query without access to its answer. TTT-NN (Hardt & Sun, 2024) finetunes on retrieved neighbors. However, its performance depends on the coverage and quality of an external corpus. Other approaches exploit the test context itself. On ARC, Akyürek et al. (2025) augment supplied inputoutput demonstrations using task-preserving transformations, relying on labeled exemplars and the structure of the grid-based domain. TTAdapt (Kaya et al., 2026) iteratively finetunes VLM on pseudolabels obtained by aggregating token probabilities across augmented versions of the test input. TLM (Hu et al., 2025) instead minimizes perplexity on unlabeled test inputs, supporting domain adaptation without explicitly supervising the reasoning required to answer particular query. More closely related, TT-SI (Acikgoz et al., 2026) finetunes an LLM on self-generated examples for tool-use queries, validating tool calls and using majority agreement to select function labels. straightforward extension to VLMs would adapt on generated text-only questionanswer pairs. SIMIT instead constructs complete multimodal examples by specifying answers before generating and verifying the corresponding images. This introduces visual realization problem across natural and structured domains, with supervision grounded in constructed visual content.

sections.content: Agentic Evaluation Protocol Task You will judge list of (image, question, answer) triplets, one at time. For each, decide: is this triplet correct? does the image actually support answering the question, and does the given answer correctly answer that question about that image? You are NOT told which method or system produced any answer, and you should not try to guess judge every triplet on its own merits, using the same standard for all of them. How to judge correctness (apply per question type) - Multiple choice (question lists lettered options): the answer is correct only if it selects the option that is actually true of the image. - Short-answer / single-word-or-phrase VQA: the answer is correct if it is reasonable, factually accurate response to the question given the image. Minor differences in phrasing, capitalization, singular/plural, or synonym that means the same thing do NOT make an answer incorrect. - Captioning (provide caption, describe the image): correct if the caption accurately describes salient, verifiable content of the image. It does not need to match any specific reference wording, and does not need to describe every detail it needs to not be wrong or fabricated. - Document / chart / infographic QA: the answer must match what is actually shown in or computable from the image (a number, label, or short text span). Treat this like short-answer VQA otherwise. - Unanswerable / cannot be determined as the given answer: correct ONLY if the image genuinely does not contain enough information to answer the question. If the image clearly does support an answer, Unanswerable is INCORRECT. What to ignore Cosmetic image imperfections (slightly off rendering, minor visual artifacts, mild blur/upscaling, imperfect but legible text) are irrelevant UNLESS they actually obscure or change the information needed to answer the question. Judge the content, not the production quality. When to flag ambiguous instead of deciding Use flagged_ambiguous: true sparingly only when careful, reasonable person genuinely could not decide correct-vs-incorrect (e.g., the image failed to load / is corrupted, the question itself is nonsensical or untranslatable, or the answer is genuine judgment call with real ambiguity). Do NOT use it just because question is hard, or because you are not 100% certain make your best judgment call in those cases instead and explain why in the rationale. Ambiguous items are excluded from the statistics and reported separately, so overusing this flag would throw away real signal. Output format Exactly one JSON object per line (JSONL), one line per input triplet, in any order, written to the exact output path youre given: {"audit_id": "<copied from input>", "verdict": true, "flagged_ambiguous": false, "rationale": "<one short sentence>"} verdict: true = correct triplet, false = incorrect triplet. rationale: one short sentence explaining the call (or the ambiguity, if flagged). Every input triplet must get exactly one output line. REAL DATA: ADDITIONAL ANALYSES How much can additional synthetic data improve performance, and when does it match humanannotated data? We compare the two supervision sources across three adaptation settings, then examine whether they benefit the same benchmarks. Experimental Setup. We pair each synthetic-data method with its real-data counterpart: SIMIT-ICL with retrieved in-context demonstrations (RICES), SIMIT-FT (Single-Query) with finetuning on retrieved neighbors (TTT-NN), and SIMIT-FT (Test-Set) with supervised finetuning on the real-data pool. These comparisons use the same adaptation procedure but different supervision sources. The real-data methods have access to human annotations and, for retrieval, an external embedding model. They therefore serve as privileged reference methods outside our self-contained setting, rather than label-free baselines. To compare the sources at identical sample counts, we disable dynamic mechanisms in our pipeline: adaptive budget allocation (ABA) and difficulty filtering (DF). ABA varies the number of generated candidates across queries, while DF changes how many are retained according to their difficulty. Keeping either enabled would mix the effect of adding samples with that of selecting or allocating them. We instead use fixed count for every query, while retaining the other synthesis components, including verification. Throughout this section, unfiltered means that DF is disabled; it does not mean that samples are unverified. Because this comparison disables two important components of our pipeline, these results should not be interpreted as the performance of the full SIMIT pipeline. With ABA and DF, SIMIT achieves approximately 6.4% mean relative gain over zero-shot, compared with 4.35% when both are disabled (Tab. 2). For each supervision source, we fit linear model predicting the performance gain from the zero-shot score. We then subtract the predicted gain from the observed gain and correlate these residuals across the two sources. This tests whether benchmarks that benefit more than expected from real data also benefit more than expected from synthetic data. The correlation remains strong even after this adjustment: pooled = 0.83, compared with = 0.90 before adjustment. Within each setting, the residual correlations are = 0.79 for ICL, = 0.93 for test-set finetuning, and = 0.77 for single-query finetuning (all < 0.01). Thus, linear relationship with zero-shot performance does not fully explain the association between realand synthetic-data gains. Where Do the Sources Differ? Real data generally provides larger gains, particularly on Doc. & Infographic tasks. However, synthetic data outperforms real data on Math & Science under both finetuning settings, showing that query-conditioned generation can sometimes provide more useful supervision than retrieved examples. Synthetic data also offers more consistent benefits under single-query adaptation. TTT-NN produces large gains on some benchmarks but substantial regressions on others, consistent with retrieved examples sometimes being poorly matched to the target query. SIMIT-FT (Single-Query) can also regress, but its worst-case decline is smaller, and it outperforms its real-data counterpart on more benchmarks than in either of the other adaptation settings. These results suggest that queryconditioned synthesis provides more reliable supervision when adapting to an individual query with only few examples. Implications. These findings are consistent with SIMIT rehearsing and reorganizing existing capabilities through targeted supervision, while remaining limited by what the model can reliably generate. Its advantage on Math & Science under finetuning, alongside real datas stronger gains elsewhere, suggests complementary strengths: query-specific practice from synthesis and broader visual and factual coverage from real data. Real and synthetic data offer complementary benefits. Real examples provide authentic content but depend on the coverage of the available pool and the quality of retrieval. Synthetic examples can target each query and vary in difficulty, but may contain realization errors or redundant content. Diminishing returns from unfiltered synthesis should consequently not be treated as an intrinsic ceiling on synthetic supervision: sample count alone does not capture how much valid, informative support the data provide. The gains from ABA and DF reinforce this distinction. sections.title: N QUALITATIVE RESULTS
sections.content: Figs. 15 25 present selected qualitative examples with ABA and DF disabled and fixed sample budget of = 2 for compact visualization. We compare adaptation using retrieved real samples (RICES and TTT-NN) with self-generated synthetic samples (SIMIT-ICL and SIMIT-FT (SQ)). These examples illustrate how self-generated samples can yield more accurate answers. The examples also suggest greater sensitivity to mismatched supervision under fine-tuning. In Fig. 20 (bottom), TTT-NN output adds the unnecessary attributes tan and white, echoing tan in the first retrieved sample, whereas RICES answers dog. Similarly, in Fig. 21 (top), TTT-NN repeats the retrieved material label porcelain when asked to identify an art form. These cases suggest that fine-tuning can sometimes absorb irrelevant details from retrieved supervision, while ICL can disregard them. Synthetic supervision nevertheless remains imperfect. In Fig. 20 (bottom), the first synthetic answer labels the animals belly pink, although its belly is not clearly visible. This unsupported attribute differs from the target task of recognizing the animal, and both SIMIT variants still answer correctly. The example illustrates that noisy synthetic label need not reinforce the target prediction error or prevent successful adaptation. Sec. 4.4 examines this distinction quantitatively by measuring the alignment between supervision errors and the models existing failures. sections.title: O LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORKS
sections.content: SIMIT-FTICL just uses the SIMIT-FT (Test-Set) checkpoint in place of the pretrained baseline model in the SIMIT-ICL procedure. We apply this combination without additional hyperparameter tuning and any dedicated training on synthetic samples formatted for in-context learning. Both directions can improve the accuracy even more. SIMIT is orthogonal to LFRL methods, suggesting that combining both approaches could yield further gains in suitable domains. SIMIT could also be used to augment real training data with similar synthetic samples. Our self-generated synthetic samples are tailored for the expected target distribution and the models learning capacity. CRAFT (Ziegler et al., 2025) demonstrates that small set of human-curated examples can guide the construction of much larger task-specific synthetic dataset for finetuning. SEAL (Zweiger et al., 2025) also supports this paradigm by providing human-learning analogy: students rewrite raw material from lectures, textbooks, and online sources into their own notes to internalize the content and better answer exam questions. SIMIT performs query-conditioned, transductive test-time adaptation through constructive selfsupervision, producing local-optimal models specialized for given target test set. Such specialization can reduce performance on other benchmarks, as illustrated in Fig. 11. Transferring these capabilities to generalist model could therefore benefit from multi-teacher on-policy distillation across specialists (Ma et al., 2026), strategy popularized by DeepSeek-V4 (Xu et al., 2026). Future work could explore jointly updating the solver and synthesizer. We keep the synthesizer fixed to preserve broad applicability and enable rigorous controlled ablations of the proposed design choices. In particular, SIMIT-ICL requires no training and can improve fixed models, including closed-source proprietary models accessible only through an API.
